post.caption: Bahrain bans the sale of cultured pearls. Bahrain was the center of the Gulf pearl trade, and divers went out for about four months each summer. They wore a nose clip and leather caps on their fingers, and a stone weight on a rope pulled them down to the oysters. The merchants who bought the pearls were called tawash. In the 1930s, cultured pearls from Japan helped end the old trade. In 2012, UNESCO listed Bahrain's pearling path as a World Heritage site, and Bahrain's DANAT lab tells natural pearls from cultured ones. Today, cultured pearls are barred from its jewelry counters.
